scope: The first ten selected contextual Mark spot checks; review of linked separately hosted full works or labelled original-work excerpts. Browsable Migne and historical translations, not modern critical editions. Not a claim of Greek/Latin critical collation.
editorialPolicy: Canonical Oxford/Newman Catena text and inherited Father labels must be loaded unchanged from the approved pack. The external witness is provenance/context evidence, not alternative dialogue or an importable text corpus. Never promote these records to publication without independent editorial approval and acceptance of attribution, context, translation and rights.

rows.editorialQuestion: Why does Jesus seem to pass by the frightened disciples?
rows.witnessAnchor: His wish to pass by those persons
rows.contextFinding: The seeming passage-by is discussed as eliciting their cry for help, not evidence that Jesus would abandon the apostles.
rows.readerGuard: Do not transform Augustine's theological interpretation into a reported Gospel event.

rows.editorialQuestion: How can wealthy people enter the kingdom if riches endanger salvation?
rows.contextFinding: The full Latin discussion supports both detachment from riches and Christ/camel Passion typology, and continues into conversion by grace.
rows.readerGuard: Source-text variance: the full Latin names Matthew, Zacchaeus and Joseph, while the canonical Catena excerpt omits Zacchaeus. Never silently amend the Catena or pretend the excerpt is the full original discussion.

rows.editorialQuestion: What does the angel seated on the right signify?
rows.originalWork: Gregory the Great, Homiliae in Evangelia
rows.originalWorkLocus: Book II, Homily XXI, section 2; original Latin also cross-referenced at CCSL 141
rows.witnessAnchor: Quid namque per sinistram nisi vita praesens
rows.contextFinding: Gregory explicitly opposes present life (left) to enduring life (right) in his symbolic interpretation of the angel.
rows.readerGuard: Attribute this symbolism to Gregory's homily, not the biblical narrator.

rows.editorialQuestion: How can Mark call an appearance of the risen Christ the last?
rows.witnessAnchor: Ninthly, at the time to which Mark refers in the words
rows.contextFinding: Augustine examines same-evening and fortieth-day explanations (§§75–76), then in the fuller context (§§77 and 83) favors the final pre-Ascension meal appearance; the Catena's truncated extract alone does not convey the full-work preference.
rows.readerGuard: Do not present the proposed reconciliations as equally favored by Augustine. Distinguish his eventual preference for the late, pre-Ascension appearance from a historically established event chronology; retain Thomas's absence problem.

rows.editorialQuestion: Why did Peter falter after acknowledging Jesus as Christ?
rows.witnessAnchor: the mystery of the cross and of the resurrection
rows.contextFinding: Peter's confession was revealed, while the Passion and Resurrection were still misunderstood; Chrysostom is commenting on Matthew 16.
rows.readerGuard: Identify the original homily as Matthew, not as an independently authored Mark homily.

rows.editorialQuestion: Why did Christ curse the fig tree when the season of figs had not arrived?
rows.witnessAnchor: For the disciples' sakes, that they might have confidence
rows.contextFinding: The fig-tree sign displays authority and readiness for the Passion; the original argument rejects treating botanical timing as the reason for punitive injustice.
rows.readerGuard: Do not claim that Chrysostom takes the tree to have moral fault or that the sign establishes a historical botanical judgment.

rows.editorialQuestion: Why does Christ say 'if possible' about deceiving the elect?
rows.originalWork: Gregory the Great, Homiliae in Ezechielem
rows.originalWorkLocus: Book I, Homily IX, section 8; PL 76
rows.witnessAnchor: si electi sunt, fieri non potest
rows.contextFinding: Gregory interprets the conditional as the elect's trembling in temptation without falling, using the parallel in Matthew 24:24.
rows.readerGuard: Keep the conditional and perseverance nuance; Gregory's Ezekiel homily cites the Gospel parallel, not an independent Mark commentary.

rows.editorialQuestion: Why does the Last Supper depict reclining if the Passover required standing?
rows.originalWorkLocus: Commentary on Mark 14:17–18; exact Greek column/edition not independently collated
rows.witnessLanguage: modern English excerpt of work; edition unidentified
rows.witnessAnchor: One must think that the Lord first performed the Passover
rows.contextFinding: A separately labelled Commentary on Mark excerpt restates the probable sequence, but no reliable Greek original-work witness was independently inspected.
rows.readerGuard: Retain 'probable' / 'one must think': this is Theophylact's proposed sequence, not an established fact or a verbatim independent Greek verification.

rows.editorialQuestion: How does Augustine reconcile the two thieves reviling Christ with Luke's account of one repentant thief?
rows.witnessAnchor: a certain mode of speech which is sufficiently familiar
rows.contextFinding: Augustine's plural-for-singular harmonization appears in the full work; a different proposal about both thieves is a neighboring Catena voice.
rows.readerGuard: Do not attribute the adjacent alternative about both thieves first reviling Christ to Augustine without its separately proved owner.

rows.editorialQuestion: Why identify Judas by his origin or name?
rows.originalWorkLocus: Homily 1, section 2, on distinguishing Judas Iscariot from Judas the Zealot
rows.witnessLanguage: French translation of full homily, not Greek-language collation
rows.contextFinding: The independently readable homily distinguishes the two Judases and makes an admonition against defamatory epithets.
rows.readerGuard: Do not copy the French modern translation into canonical Catena dialogue; this is not a check of the Greek critical text.
